# Levelling a tipping-bucket rain gauge

A tipping-bucket gauge that isn't sitting level will under- or over-count
rainfall in a way that looks exactly like a calibration fault, so levelling
is the first thing checked on any station visit, not a step folded into the
calibration procedure itself. This document covers the spirit-level
procedure on its own, since it comes up on its own far more often than a
full calibration pour does — after a mast is re-guyed, after a mount bracket
is swapped, or any time a gauge has been knocked while someone was working
nearby.

## Why level matters more than it looks like it should

A tipping bucket balances on a small pivot, and even a couple of degrees of
tilt shifts the point at which one side outweighs the other. Tilted toward
the funnel's low side, the bucket tips slightly early and over-counts;
tilted the other way, it holds slightly more water than it should before
tipping and under-counts. Neither failure throws an error anywhere. The
gauge keeps reporting numbers that look perfectly plausible, just wrong by a
consistent percentage, which is exactly the kind of fault that goes
unnoticed until someone compares two neighbouring stations after the same
storm and finds them disagreeing by more than rainfall alone would explain.

## What you need

A small bubble spirit level that sits flat across the gauge's rim — the
torpedo level most people already carry in a bag works fine, a phone level
app is an acceptable fallback if that's all that's on hand — plus whatever
shims the mounting bracket at that station normally takes. Some brackets use
thin washers under one or two of the fixing bolts; others have a built-in
levelling foot. Check the station card before assuming which kind is fitted.

## The procedure

1. **Set the level across the rim in one direction, then rotate ninety
   degrees and check again.** A gauge can look level checked only along one
   axis while still leaning noticeably along the other, so both directions
   have to be checked before touching anything.

2. **Loosen the fixing bolts just enough to move the gauge, not so much
   that it can shift under its own weight.** Fully removing the bolts
   invites the gauge to drop or twist while your hands are full of a level
   and a shim.

3. **Add or remove shims under the low side until the bubble sits centred
   in both directions.** Work in small steps — a single thin washer often
   makes a bigger difference than it looks like it should, and overshooting
   in the other direction just means starting again.

4. **Tighten the fixing bolts in the order the bracket was designed for,
   not just whichever is closest to hand.** Tightening opposite bolts
   alternately, a little at a time, keeps the gauge from twisting off level
   again as the last bolt goes fully home — a mistake that's easy to make
   and easy to miss until the next visit.

5. **Recheck the bubble once everything is tight.** Torquing down the
   fixings can nudge a gauge that was level a moment ago, so the last check
   has to happen after tightening, not before.

## When to check it without being asked

Every full calibration pour starts with this check, but it's also worth
doing any time a mast has been re-guyed nearby, after any bracket swap, and
after high wind has been reported at that station even if nothing looks
obviously disturbed. A gauge that's drifted out of level rarely announces
itself, and a thirty-second check costs far less than a season of
quietly wrong rainfall figures.
